title: How a nuclear war starts: Second-by-second timeline | Annie Jacobsen and Lex Fridman
summary: Annie Jacobsen walks Lex Fridman through how a US-Russia nuclear war would unfold minute by minute, from launch on warning and sole presidential authority to billions dead in nuclear winter.

assertions.quote: And then comes nuclear winter where the billions happen from starvation.
In the position of the president, it's almost inevitable that they have to respond.
you can just start a nuclear war if you are the commander in chief, the President of the United States
it means the United States will not wait to absorb a nuclear attack.

verdicts.note: The US keeps ICBMs ready to launch under attack and decision times of minutes are widely cited, though official policy says it does not rely on launch on warning.

The paper describes NORAD briefing the President and Secretary of Defense, who must decide before a use-it-or-lose-it point with decision times from about half an hour down to near zero; it notes uncertainty, possibly deliberate, about which posture the US actually uses, and its data are from 2013.

SIPRI says the US has what can be described as a launch-on-warning or launch-under-attack posture, launching ICBMs before attacking warheads detonate; the exact minutes available to the president are not given here.

assertions.quote: We are one misunderstanding, one miscalculation away
we're closer to this as a reality than ever before.

verdicts.note: The Doomsday Clock is at its closest ever and arms control has lapsed, but forecasters do not rate today's risk above the Cold War's worst crises.

The Clock's record 85 seconds is later than any Cold War setting, but the setting blends nuclear with climate, bio and AI risk; the nuclear section describes a worsening slide, not a quantified comparison with the Cold War.

assertions.quote: the ICBMs cannot be recalled or redirected once launched.

verdicts.note: US ICBMs have no recall or self-destruct mechanism after launch.
